overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how a language model takes in text and produces a reply. You'll be asked about tokens and tokenization, embeddings, next-token prediction, and sampling and temperature.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A chatbot is asked how many times the letter "r" appears in a long word, and it gives the wrong count. Which feature of language models best explains the difficulty?

options.html: The model's training data left out spelling
options.text: The model's training data left out spelling
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Training text contains a great deal about spelling. The difficulty comes from tokens: the model receives a word as one or a few tokens and doesn't directly see its letters.

options.html: The model receives tokens and not single letters
options.text: The model receives tokens and not single letters
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A word reaches the model as one token or a few, and the letters inside a token aren't visible to it as separate items.

options.html: The model samples its letters at a high temperature
options.text: The model samples its letters at a high temperature
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Temperature affects which token is chosen and doesn't explain trouble with letters. The model receives a word as one or a few tokens and doesn't directly see its letters.

options.html: The model keeps only the first letter of each word
options.text: The model keeps only the first letter of each word
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Models don't store first letters. The model receives a word as one or a few tokens and doesn't directly see its letters.

forms.stemHtml: In a set of word embeddings, "coffee" and "tea" sit close together. What produced that closeness?

options.html: Engineers placed related words near each other by hand
options.text: Engineers placed related words near each other by hand
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nobody assigns the positions. They're learned in training, and words used in similar contexts end up near each other.

options.html: The two words share most of their letters
options.text: The two words share most of their letters
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Embeddings reflect how words are used, and spelling plays no part. Words used in similar contexts end up near each other.

options.html: A dictionary lists the two words as related terms
options.text: A dictionary lists the two words as related terms
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No dictionary is consulted. Positions are learned in training, and words used in similar contexts end up near each other.

options.html: Training on text that uses the two in similar ways
options.text: Training on text that uses the two in similar ways
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Embeddings are learned. Tokens that are used in similar ways are pushed toward similar positions because that improves the model's predictions.

forms.stemHtml: Given the text so far, what does a language model produce before any token is chosen?

options.html: A likelihood for every token in its vocabulary
options.text: A likelihood for every token in its vocabulary
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The model's output is a full ranking of possible next tokens. Choosing one from it is a separate step.

options.html: A complete draft of the reply for later release
options.text: A complete draft of the reply for later release
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The model has no finished reply in hand. It produces a likelihood for every token in its vocabulary, one position at a time.

options.html: The single correct next word and nothing else
options.text: The single correct next word and nothing else
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The model doesn't output one answer. It produces a likelihood for every token in its vocabulary.

options.html: A list of stored passages that match the question
options.text: A list of stored passages that match the question
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The model doesn't look passages up. It produces a likelihood for every token in its vocabulary.

forms.stemHtml: A product team raises the temperature setting on their chatbot. What change should they expect in its replies?

options.html: Replies will become identical from one run to the next
options.text: Replies will become identical from one run to the next
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the effect of the lowest temperature. Raising the temperature makes less likely tokens get picked more often, so replies vary more.

options.html: Replies will be checked against facts before they appear
options.text: Replies will be checked against facts before they appear
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Temperature has nothing to do with fact-checking. Raising it makes less likely tokens get picked more often, so replies vary more.

options.html: Replies will vary more and use less likely wording
options.text: Replies will vary more and use less likely wording
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Temperature controls how often sampling picks less likely tokens. A higher setting gives more varied and more surprising text.

options.html: Replies will be split into a larger number of tokens
options.text: Replies will be split into a larger number of tokens
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Temperature doesn't affect how text is split into tokens. Raising it makes less likely tokens get picked more often, so replies vary more.

forms.stemHtml: You ask a chatbot the same question in two new conversations and get two different replies. Which of these help explain why? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The next token is chosen partly by chance
options.text: The next token is chosen partly by chance
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Sampling picks among likely tokens by chance, weighted by likelihood, so two runs can pick differently.

options.html: Each chosen token changes the input for later ones
options.text: Each chosen token changes the input for later ones
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Every chosen token is added to the text, so one different early choice leads to different predictions afterward.

options.html: The model's parameters change between the two conversations
options.text: The model's parameters change between the two conversations
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The parameters stay fixed while you use the model. The variation comes from chance in choosing tokens.

options.html: The model ranks the candidates differently for the same text
options.text: The model ranks the candidates differently for the same text
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The ranking for a given text is the same each time. What differs is the draw from that ranking.

options.html: Several continuations can be about equally likely
options.text: Several continuations can be about equally likely
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Where the ranking is spread across several options, chance has more room to change the reply.

title: Tokens, meaning, and next-token prediction
